igcse-0580-percentages-amounts.description: Choose the whole, calculate a percentage of a quantity and compare two amounts using a common unit.

sections.title: Where does the hundred come from?
sections.label: A share of the whole
sections.intro: The whole amount is 100 percent. Before working out a share, decide which quantity the question treats as the whole.

blocks.html: Without a calculator, find \(10\%\) by dividing by 10. Halve this for \(5\%\). Alternatively, multiply the full amount by \(\frac{p}{100}\) for \(p\%\).

figure.alt: Ten equal sections represent the whole. Three are shaded to mark three tenths.
figure.caption: Each of the ten equal sections represents ten percent of the whole.

blocks.title: Find a percentage mentally
blocks.prompt: Work out \(55\%\) of \(1620\) litres without a calculator.
blocks.hint: Find ten percent and halve it to get five percent.
blocks.solution:
\(1620\) litres is the full amount, or \(100\%\).

A tenth of the amount is \(162\) and half of that is \(81\), so each \(5\%\) is \(81\) litres.

Use \(11\) of those five-percent units. The answer is \(891\) litres.

retry.feedback: The task asks for the stated part of the whole, so use the given percentage directly.

blocks.html: A deposit or part of a quantity uses the stated share. A question asking for what is left uses the complementary share.

blocks.title: Find the deposit
blocks.prompt: The deposit for booking a room is \(29\%\) of a booking cost of £126. Find the deposit in pounds.
blocks.hint: Divide the percentage number by 100 to find the multiplier for the amount requested.
blocks.solution:
The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{29}{100}=0.29\) of it.

\(126\times0.29=36.54\).

So the required amount is £36.54.

retry.feedback: The task asks for the stated part of the whole, so use the given percentage directly.

blocks.html: For a price, record the final amount in pounds with two decimal places when it is not a whole number.

sections.title: What can percentages below 1 or above 100 mean?
sections.label: Small and large percentages
sections.intro: Use the same multiplication rule even when the rate lies outside the range you usually meet. A comparison can exceed 100 percent.

blocks.html: \(138\%=1.38\) means a quantity greater than the reference amount. \(0.6\%=0.006\) means a small fraction of the reference.

blocks.title: Calculate more than 100 percent
blocks.prompt: A route is \(40\) m long. A longer route measures \(123\%\) of this length. Find the longer route’s length in metres.
blocks.hint: Divide the percentage number by 100 to find the multiplier for the amount requested.
blocks.solution:
The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{123}{100}=1.23\) of it.

\(40\times1.23=49.2\).

So the required amount is \(49.2\) metres.

retry.feedback: A percentage above 100 includes the full original amount as well as the extra part.

blocks.html: The number before the percent sign must be divided by 100. Applying \(0.6\) would calculate \(60\%\), which is one hundred times too large for \(0.6\%\).

blocks.title: Use a small decimal percentage
blocks.prompt: A dry mix has mass \(1160\) kg. A colour additive makes up \(2.75\%\) of that mass. Find the mass of the additive in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Divide the percentage number by 100 to find the multiplier for the amount requested.
blocks.solution:
The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{2.75}{100}=0.0275\) of it.

\(1160\times0.0275=31.9\).

So the required amount is \(31.9\) kilograms.

retry.feedback: The task asks for the stated part of the whole, so use the given percentage directly.

blocks.html: Estimate the size before calculating. A part described as less than one percent should be less than one hundredth of the reference.

sections.title: How do I turn two quantities into a percentage?
sections.label: Choose the denominator
sections.intro: A question that gives two amounts and asks for a percentage is asking for a ratio. Identify which amount is the comparison base.

blocks.html: Match the units, divide the part by the stated reference and multiply by 100. If a total has two disjoint parts, add them first to get the denominator.

blocks.title: Compare a length with a longer reference
blocks.prompt: A strand is \(4800\) cm long. Express its length as a percentage of \(100\) m. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Convert the reference to centimetres before forming the ratio.
blocks.solution:
Use the same units. The reference length in centimetres is \(10000\).

Divide the strand length by the reference length. \(\frac{4800}{10000}\times100=48\).

The strand is \(48\%\) of the reference length.

retry.feedback: Put both lengths into the same unit before using their ratio.

blocks.html: The part mentioned first does not necessarily give the denominator. Look for the full group or the value after ‘as a percentage of’.

blocks.title: Identify the whole before finding a percentage
blocks.prompt: A collection contains \(3510\) labelled specimens and \(990\) unlabelled specimens. What percentage of the collection is labelled? Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: The denominator is the complete group, so add both counts first.
blocks.solution:
The whole collection contains \(3510+990=4500\) specimens.

Compare the labelled specimens with the whole. \(\frac{3510}{4500}\times100=78\).

The labelled percentage is \(78\%\).

retry.feedback: That percentage describes the unlabelled specimens. Use the labelled count on top.

blocks.html: State the common units you used. They cancel in the ratio, so the result needs a percent sign on paper.

examples.title: Find a percentage mentally
examples.question: Work out \(15\%\) of \(260\) litres without a calculator.
solution: \(260\) litres is the full amount, or \(100\%\).
A tenth of the amount is \(26\) and half of that is \(13\), so each \(5\%\) is \(13\) litres.
Use \(3\) of those five-percent units. The answer is \(39\) litres.

examples.title: Find the deposit
examples.question: The deposit for booking a room is \(22\%\) of a booking cost of £176. Find the deposit in pounds.
solution: The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{22}{100}=0.22\) of it.

examples.title: Calculate more than 100 percent
examples.question: A route is \(290\) m long. A longer route measures \(118\%\) of this length. Find the longer route’s length in metres.
solution: The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{118}{100}=1.18\) of it.

examples.title: Use a small decimal percentage
examples.question: A dry mix has mass \(2160\) kg. A colour additive makes up \(2.25\%\) of that mass. Find the mass of the additive in kilograms.
solution: The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{2.25}{100}=0.0225\) of it.

examples.title: Compare a length with a longer reference
examples.question: A strand is \(9450\) cm long. Express its length as a percentage of \(225\) m.
solution: Use the same units. The reference length in centimetres is \(22500\).
Divide the strand length by the reference length. \(\frac{9450}{22500}\times100=42\).
The strand is \(42\%\) of the reference length.

examples.title: Identify the whole before finding a percentage
examples.question: A collection contains \(4830\) labelled specimens and \(2170\) unlabelled specimens. What percentage of the collection is labelled?
solution: Compare the labelled specimens with the whole. \(\frac{4830}{7000}\times100=69\).

extraPractice.title: Calculate more than 100 percent
extraPractice.prompt: A route is \(720\) m long. A longer route measures \(135\%\) of this length. Find the longer route’s length in metres.
extraPractice.hint: Divide the percentage number by 100 to find the multiplier for the amount requested.
extraPractice.solution:
The reference amount is \(100\%\). Use \(\frac{135}{100}=1.35\) of it.

\(720\times1.35=972\).

extraPractice.hint: Convert the reference to centimetres before forming the ratio.

extraPractice.title: Identify the whole before finding a percentage
extraPractice.prompt: A collection contains \(1720\) labelled specimens and \(280\) unlabelled specimens. What percentage of the collection is labelled? Enter the number before the percent sign.

revision.examTip: Before calculating, check that you have identified the intended reference amount.

igcse-0580-percentages-increase-decrease.description: Choose a forward multiplier and distinguish the amount of a change from the final amount.

sections.title: How do I find the new amount?
sections.label: Begin with 100 percent
sections.intro: Start by deciding whether the amount increases or decreases. The old value represents 100 percent either way.

blocks.html: For a rate of \(p\%\), the increase multiplier is \(1+\frac{p}{100}\) and the decrease multiplier is \(1-\frac{p}{100}\). A single multiplication gives the final amount.

figure.alt: The starting bar is shown whole. A forward increase adds a piece. A forward decrease removes a piece from the starting length.
figure.caption: An increase adds to the original bar. A decrease keeps what remains after the loss.

blocks.title: Find the new volume after an increase
blocks.prompt: A storage tank initially holds \(160\) litres. The volume of water is increased by \(8\%\). Find the new volume of water in litres.
blocks.hint: Begin with 100 percent. Add for an increase or subtract for a decrease before writing the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
An increase makes the new value \(108\%\) of the starting value.

The corresponding multiplier is \(1.08\).

\(160\times1.08=172.8\).

The requested amount is \(172.8\) litres.

retry.feedback: That is the amount of the change. The task asks for the amount after the change.

blocks.html: The multiplier for a decrease by \(18\%\) is \(0.82\). Multiplying by \(0.18\) gives the amount removed.

blocks.title: Find what remains after a decrease
blocks.prompt: A reservoir contains \(1080\) litres. It loses \(18\%\) of that water. Find the remaining volume in litres.
blocks.hint: Begin with 100 percent. Add for an increase or subtract for a decrease before writing the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
A decrease leaves \(82\%\) of the starting value.

The corresponding multiplier is \(0.82\).

\(1080\times0.82=885.6\).

The requested amount is \(885.6\) litres.

retry.feedback: That is the amount of the change. The task asks for the amount after the change.

blocks.html: Check that an increase gives an answer above the original and a decrease gives one below it.

sections.title: How do profit and discounts change a price?
sections.label: Cost, sale and discount
sections.intro: Name the price that is 100 percent before using a multiplier. In a profit calculation this is the cost price.

blocks.html: A profit on cost increases the cost price. A discount on an advertised price decreases the advertised price. Use the correct initial price in each calculation.

blocks.title: Apply a profit percentage to the cost price
blocks.prompt: A trader buys a restored lamp for £260. The selling price gives a profit of \(14\%\) of the cost price. Find the selling price in pounds.
blocks.hint: Begin with 100 percent. Add for an increase or subtract for a decrease before writing the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
An increase makes the new value \(114\%\) of the starting value.

The corresponding multiplier is \(1.14\).

\(260\times1.14=296.4\).

The requested amount is £296.40.

retry.feedback: That is the amount of the change. The task asks for the amount after the change.

blocks.html: Profit in pounds and selling price in pounds are two different results. Profit is the difference between the cost price and the selling price.

blocks.title: Find a sale price after a discount
blocks.prompt: A framed map originally costs £490. The shop reduces this price by \(24\%\). Find the sale price in pounds.
blocks.hint: Begin with 100 percent. Add for an increase or subtract for a decrease before writing the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
A decrease leaves \(76\%\) of the starting value.

The corresponding multiplier is \(0.76\).

\(490\times0.76=372.4\).

The requested amount is £372.40.

retry.feedback: That is the amount of the change. The task asks for the amount after the change.

blocks.html: Record what your last number represents. A final amount, a profit and a discount should each be clearly named.

sections.title: How can I tell whether to find a part or a new total?
sections.label: Read the quantity asked for
sections.intro: Read the last sentence before choosing the multiplier. The question might ask for the amount needed, the balance after a deposit or a longer duration.

blocks.html: A deposit of \(24\%\) leaves \(76\%\) to pay. For an increase by a decimal percentage such as \(4.5\%\), the full multiplier is \(1.045\).

blocks.title: Find the balance after a deposit
blocks.prompt: A travel group pays a deposit of \(18\%\) on a total hire cost of £380. Find how much remains to pay in pounds.
blocks.hint: Begin with 100 percent. Add for an increase or subtract for a decrease before writing the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
Once the deposit is paid, the share still to pay is \(82\%\).

The corresponding multiplier is \(0.82\).

\(380\times0.82=311.6\).

The requested amount is £311.60.

retry.feedback: That is the amount of the change. The task asks for the amount after the change.

blocks.html: If \(4.5\%\) becomes \(1.45\), a decimal place has moved. Check the expected size of the increase.

blocks.title: Apply an increase by a fractional percentage
blocks.prompt: A timed equipment trial runs for \(610\) minutes. A second trial is planned to run for \(17.5\%\) longer than the first. Find the planned duration of the second trial in minutes.
blocks.hint: Begin with 100 percent. Add for an increase or subtract for a decrease before writing the multiplier.
blocks.solution:
An increase makes the new value \(117.5\%\) of the starting value.

The corresponding multiplier is \(1.175\).

\(610\times1.175=716.75\).

The requested amount is \(716.75\) minutes.

retry.feedback: That is the amount of the change. The task asks for the amount after the change.

blocks.html: Write the unit beside your final answer. Keep the full multiplier while you work.

examples.title: Find the new volume after an increase
examples.question: A storage tank initially holds \(1160\) litres. The volume of water is increased by \(6\%\). Find the new volume of water in litres.
solution: An increase makes the new value \(106\%\) of the starting value.

examples.title: Find what remains after a decrease

solution: A decrease leaves \(84\%\) of the starting value.

solution: A decrease leaves \(78\%\) of the starting value.

solution: Once the deposit is paid, the share still to pay is \(84\%\).

solution: An increase makes the new value \(112.5\%\) of the starting value.

igcse-0580-percentages-change-and-points.description: Measure change relative to the original amount and distinguish percentage change from percentage-point differences.

sections.title: Which amount goes in the denominator?
sections.label: Measure change from the start
sections.intro: A percentage increase or decrease describes how large the change is compared with the starting amount.

blocks.html: \(\text{percentage change number}=\frac{\text{new}-\text{old}}{\text{old}}\times100\). The old value must be positive. A negative result denotes a decrease. In a phrase such as ‘a decrease of 12 percent’, report the positive size of the decrease.

figure.alt: Two marks sit ten percentage points apart on a percentage scale.
figure.caption: A direct gap on a percentage scale measures percentage points. Relative change adds a division by the starting rate.

blocks.title: Measure a percentage increase from data
blocks.prompt: On the first day an exhibition sells \(8400\) tickets. On the second day it sells \(9408\). Find the percentage increase in daily ticket sales. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Subtract to find the size of the change. The original value goes in the denominator.
blocks.solution:
The increase is \(1008\).

Compare this with the original amount \(8400\) rather than the final amount.

\(\frac{1008}{8400}\times100=12\): the increase is \(12\%\).

retry.feedback: Your ratio needs to be scaled by 100 to report a percentage.

blocks.html: Dividing by the final value measures a different comparison.

blocks.title: Measure a percentage decrease from data
blocks.prompt: A workshop cuts its water use from \(1500\) litres to \(1170\) litres. Find the percentage decrease in water use. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Subtract to find the size of the change. The original value goes in the denominator.
blocks.solution:
The decrease is \(330\).

Compare this with the original amount \(1500\) rather than the final amount.

\(\frac{330}{1500}\times100=22\): the decrease is \(22\%\).

retry.feedback: Your ratio needs to be scaled by 100 to report a percentage.

blocks.html: Give the direction requested. If the question already says ‘percentage decrease’, give its size as a positive percentage.

sections.title: Are percentage points and percentage change the same?
sections.label: Choose between two comparisons
sections.intro: When both measurements are themselves percentages, read whether the question asks for the gap on the scale or the relative change from the earlier rate.

blocks.html: A rate rising from \(40\%\) to \(50\%\) rises by ten percentage points. Relative to \(40\%\), the increase is \(\frac{10}{40}\times 100=25\), or \(25\%\).

blocks.title: Distinguish percentage points from a relative change
blocks.prompt: The percentage of train journeys arriving on time rises from \(25.5\%\) to \(31.875\%\). Find the increase in percentage points.
blocks.hint: Read the wording to choose a difference in points or a ratio relative to the earlier percentage.
blocks.solution:
The difference is \(31.875-25.5=6.375\) percentage points.

The question asks for the difference between two percentages.

Report \(6.375\) percentage points.

retry.feedback: A difference in percentage points and a percentage change are different comparisons. Follow the instruction about the base.

blocks.html: Subtracting the two rates gives a difference in percentage points. To report a relative percentage change, divide that difference by the earlier rate.

blocks.title: Distinguish percentage points from a relative change
blocks.prompt: The percentage of train journeys arriving on time rises from \(37.5\%\) to \(50.625\%\). Find the percentage increase relative to the original on-time percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Read the wording to choose a difference in points or a ratio relative to the earlier percentage.
blocks.solution:
The difference is \(50.625-37.5=13.125\) percentage points.

For a relative increase, the original percentage is the base. \(\frac{13.125}{37.5}\times100=35\).

Report \(35\%\).

retry.feedback: A difference in percentage points and a percentage change are different comparisons. Follow the instruction about the base.

blocks.html: Use the words ‘percentage points’ for the direct gap, and the percent symbol for the relative percentage.

sections.title: Can equal changes have different percentage effects?
sections.label: Identify the base in each case
sections.intro: A change of the same size has a larger proportional effect on a smaller starting value. In a percentage loss calculation, the starting value is the price originally paid.

blocks.html: Compute each change over its own starting value. To compare the two resulting percentages, find their difference in percentage points.

blocks.title: Compare the same amount increase on two bases
blocks.prompt: Two liquid samples gain the same volume of \(100\) litres. Sample A starts with \(500\) litres and sample B starts with \(250\) litres. By how many percentage points is B’s percentage increase greater than A’s?
blocks.hint: Find each increase as a percentage of the right starting volume. Then subtract the two percentages.
blocks.solution:
Use the original amount of each sample as its own base.

The increases are \(\frac{100}{500}\times100=20\)% for A and \(\frac{100}{250}\times100=40\)% for B.

The difference between these rates is \(20\) percentage points.

retry.feedback: The increases in litres are equal, but the two starting amounts are different.

blocks.html: Using a shared denominator for two different starting amounts can hide the actual difference in their percentage change.

blocks.title: Calculate a percentage loss
blocks.prompt: A stallholder pays £4300 for a set of equipment and sells it for £2838. Find the percentage loss on the cost price. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Subtract to find the size of the change. The original value goes in the denominator.
blocks.solution:
The decrease is \(1462\).

Compare this with the original amount \(4300\) rather than the final amount.

\(\frac{1462}{4300}\times100=34\): the loss is \(34\%\).

retry.feedback: Your ratio needs to be scaled by 100 to report a percentage.

examples.title: Measure a percentage increase from data
examples.question: On the first day an exhibition sells \(1600\) tickets. On the second day it sells \(1728\). Find the percentage increase in daily ticket sales.
solution: Compare this with the original amount \(1600\) rather than the final amount.

examples.title: Measure a percentage decrease from data
examples.question: A workshop cuts its water use from \(4000\) litres to \(3240\) litres. Find the percentage decrease in water use.
solution: Compare this with the original amount \(4000\) rather than the final amount.

examples.title: Distinguish percentage points from a relative change
examples.question: The percentage of train journeys arriving on time rises from \(38\%\) to \(46.36\%\). Find the increase in percentage points.
solution: The question asks for the difference between two percentages.

examples.title: Distinguish percentage points from a relative change
examples.question: The percentage of train journeys arriving on time rises from \(50\%\) to \(66\%\). Find the percentage increase relative to the original on-time percentage.
solution: For a relative increase, the original percentage is the base. \(\frac{16}{50}\times100=32\).

examples.title: Compare the same amount increase on two bases
examples.question: Two liquid samples gain the same volume of \(600\) litres. Sample A starts with \(3000\) litres and sample B starts with \(1500\) litres. By how many percentage points is B’s percentage increase greater than A’s?
solution: Use the original amount of each sample as its own base.
The increases are \(\frac{600}{3000}\times100=20\)% for A and \(\frac{600}{1500}\times100=40\)% for B.
The difference between these rates is \(20\) percentage points.

examples.title: Calculate a percentage loss
examples.question: A stallholder pays £6800 for a set of equipment and sells it for £4692. Find the percentage loss on the cost price.

glossary.definition: The change divided by the initial amount.
One unit of difference between two percentages.

revision.body:
Methods

MethodWhat to do
Measure change from the start\(\text{percentage change number}=\frac{\text{new}-\text{old}}{\text{old}}\times100\). The old value must be positive. A negative result denotes a decrease. In a phrase such as ‘a decrease of 12 percent’, report the positive size of the decrease.
Choose between two comparisonsA rate rising from \(40\%\) to \(50\%\) rises by ten percentage points. Relative to \(40\%\), the increase is \(\frac{10}{40}\times 100=25\), or \(25\%\).
Identify the base in each caseCompute each change over its own starting value. To compare the two resulting percentages, find their difference in percentage points.

Worked line

\(38\%-32\%=6\text{ percentage points}\)

Check yourself

A rate goes from \(32\%\) to \(38\%\). Find the relative percentage increase.

Answer \(18.75\%\)
revision.checks:
• Dividing by the final value measures a different comparison.
  • Subtracting the two rates gives a difference in percentage points. To report a relative percentage change, divide that difference by the earlier rate.
  • Using a shared denominator for two different starting amounts can hide the actual difference in their percentage change.
revision.examTip: Select the right denominator for a relative change. A percentage-point difference uses subtraction alone.

igcse-0580-percentages-reverse.description: Recover the original amount after a percentage change by undoing its forward multiplier.

sections.title: How do I recover the amount before the change?
sections.label: The given amount comes after
sections.intro: The original value is 100 percent, but in a reverse problem it is unknown. Decide which percentage of it the given amount represents.

blocks.html: If original × multiplier = result, then \(\text{original}=\frac{\text{result}}{\text{multiplier}}\). Reconstruct the forward multiplier before you divide.

figure.alt: A forward arrow from Original to Result shows multiplication. A reverse arrow shows division.
figure.caption: Reverse the direction and use division by the same forward multiplier.

blocks.title: Find the starting volume after an increase
blocks.prompt: A pump’s target volume is now \(910.2\) litres after it was increased by \(11\%\). Find the original target in litres.
blocks.hint: First decide what percentage of the original the amount in the question represents.
blocks.solution:
The amount given is \(111\%\) of the original, so its forward multiplier is \(1.11\).

The forward calculation multiplied the original by \(1.11\). Undo it by dividing by that same number.

\(\frac{910.2}{1.11}=820\). The original is \(820\) litres.

Check by multiplying \(820\) by \(1.11\) to recover \(910.2\).

retry.feedback: Using the opposite percentage starts from a different base. Divide by the original forward multiplier.

blocks.html: Increasing the reduced amount by the same rate uses the smaller amount as its base. To undo the decrease, divide by the decrease multiplier.

blocks.title: Find the starting volume after a decrease
blocks.prompt: After a \(24\%\) reduction in its water use, a system uses \(91.2\) litres. Find its water use in litres before the reduction.
blocks.hint: First decide what percentage of the original the amount in the question represents.
blocks.solution:
The amount given is \(76\%\) of the original, so its forward multiplier is \(0.76\).

The forward calculation multiplied the original by \(0.76\). Undo it by dividing by that same number.

\(\frac{91.2}{0.76}=120\). The original is \(120\) litres.

Check by multiplying \(120\) by \(0.76\) to recover \(91.2\).

retry.feedback: Using the opposite percentage starts from a different base. Divide by the original forward multiplier.

blocks.html: Multiply your answer by the forward multiplier once more. You should recover the amount in the question.

sections.title: What if the amount supplied is just one part?
sections.label: Recover 100 percent
sections.intro: Sometimes the question tells you the amount of the change or a percentage share. Neither is automatically the new total.

blocks.html: If the share itself is \(p\%\) of the old amount, divide that share by \(\frac{p}{100}\). You can also find one percent by dividing by \(p\) and multiply by 100.

blocks.title: Recover the whole from a percentage share
blocks.prompt: \(18\%\) of a water tank’s capacity is \(169.2\) litres. Find its full capacity in litres.
blocks.hint: First decide what percentage of the original the amount in the question represents.
blocks.solution:
The supplied amount represents only \(18\%\) of the original.

The forward calculation multiplied the original by \(0.18\). Undo it by dividing by that same number.

\(\frac{169.2}{0.18}=940\). The original is \(940\) litres.

retry.feedback: The given value is already a percentage share. Divide by that percentage multiplier to recover the full amount.

blocks.html: An increase of \(18\%\) does not mean the given increase amount is \(118\%\) of the starting value. The new total would be \(118\%\).

blocks.title: Recover the original from a stated increase amount
blocks.prompt: A pathway is extended by \(42\%\). The increase in length is \(151.2\) m. Find the pathway’s length in metres before the extension.
blocks.hint: First decide what percentage of the original the amount in the question represents.
blocks.solution:
The supplied amount represents only \(42\%\) of the original.

The forward calculation multiplied the original by \(0.42\). Undo it by dividing by that same number.

\(\frac{151.2}{0.42}=360\). The original is \(360\) metres.

retry.feedback: The given value is already a percentage share. Divide by that percentage multiplier to recover the full amount.

blocks.html: Name the known amount in your working as ‘share’, ‘change’ or ‘new total’ before choosing the multiplier.

sections.title: How can I reverse a discount or a profit?
sections.label: Prices before a change
sections.intro: Sale and selling prices come after a change from an earlier amount. ‘Price before the discount’ and ‘cost price’ ask for the earlier figure.

blocks.html: For a sale price, divide by the fraction of the original that remains. For a selling price with profit, divide by a multiplier above 1.

blocks.title: Recover the price before a discount
blocks.prompt: A bike bag costs £54.60 after a \(22\%\) discount. Find the original price in pounds.
blocks.hint: First decide what percentage of the original the amount in the question represents.
blocks.solution:
The amount given is \(78\%\) of the original, so its forward multiplier is \(0.78\).

Divide the supplied amount by \(78\) to find 1 percent, then multiply by 100.

\(\frac{54.6}{0.78}=70\). The original is £70.00.

Check by multiplying \(70\) by \(0.78\) to recover \(54.6\).

retry.feedback: Using the opposite percentage starts from a different base. Divide by the original forward multiplier.

blocks.html: Subtracting the profit percentage from the selling price uses the wrong base. The stated profit was measured on cost price.

blocks.title: Recover the cost price from a profit
blocks.prompt: A retailer sells a refurbished chair for £408.00 at a profit of \(36\%\) on its cost price. Find the cost price in pounds.
blocks.hint: First decide what percentage of the original the amount in the question represents.
blocks.solution:
The amount given is \(136\%\) of the original, so its forward multiplier is \(1.36\).

The forward calculation multiplied the original by \(1.36\). Undo it by dividing by that same number.

\(\frac{408}{1.36}=300\). The original is £300.00.

Check by multiplying \(300\) by \(1.36\) to recover \(408\).

retry.feedback: Using the opposite percentage starts from a different base. Divide by the original forward multiplier.

blocks.html: Check the direction. Before a discount the amount was higher. Before a profit was added, the cost price was lower.

igcse-0580-percentages-successive.description: Follow changing bases, combine multipliers, report the overall change and work backwards from a final amount.

sections.title: What does the second percentage apply to?
sections.label: Change the base at each stage
sections.intro: Apply the first change to the starting value. The result is the starting value for the next stage.

blocks.html: Multiply by the first factor, then the second. The single equivalent multiplier is their product.

figure.alt: Start, after the first change and finish appear in three separate boxes, linked by arrows.
figure.caption: The second arrow starts at the updated amount.

blocks.title: Apply an increase followed by a decrease
blocks.prompt: The starting volume in a tank is \(400\) litres. It is increased by \(12\%\), then the updated volume decreases by \(9\%\). Find the final volume in litres.
blocks.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is \(1.12\) and the second is \(0.91\).

The combined multiplier is \(1.12\times0.91=1.0192\).

\(400\times1.0192=407.68\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

blocks.html: Adding the rates treats both changes as amounts taken on the same original base. Successive changes normally use different bases.

blocks.title: Use two decreases on different bases
blocks.prompt: A batch starts with mass \(2900\) kg. Stage 1 reduces its mass by \(22\%\). Stage 2 reduces the remaining mass by \(20\%\). Find the mass after both drying stages in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is \(0.78\) and the second is \(0.8\).

The combined multiplier is \(0.78\times0.8=0.624\).

\(2900\times0.624=1809.6\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

blocks.html: Write a stage arrow or one multiplication for each stated change. Keep exact intermediate values where practical.

sections.title: How do I decide the overall percentage change?
sections.label: Compare the product with 1
sections.intro: The final amount is the initial amount multiplied by the product of the stage multipliers. That product describes the fraction of the original that remains.

blocks.html: Above 1 means a net increase, and below 1 means a net decrease. Subtract the smaller of the product and 1 from the larger and multiply by 100 for the size of the change.

blocks.title: Calculate the net change after equal rates
blocks.prompt: The size of an image file first increases by \(6\%\). The resulting size then decreases by \(6\%\). Find the overall percentage decrease from the original size. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is \(1.06\) and the second is \(0.94\).

The combined multiplier is \(1.06\times0.94=0.9964\).

The final value is \(99.64\%\) of the original, so the overall decrease is \(0.36\%\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

blocks.html: An increase and a decrease at the same rate do not return you to the start. The decrease uses the increased base.

blocks.title: Interpret the product of two reductions
blocks.prompt: A supplier reduces a packaging fee by \(13.25\%\). The reduced fee is then cut by a further \(30\%\). Find the overall percentage decrease. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is \(0.8675\) and the second is \(0.7\).

The combined multiplier is \(0.8675\times0.7=0.60725\).

The final value is \(60.725\%\) of the original, so the overall decrease is \(39.275\%\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

blocks.html: A combined multiplier of \(0.942\) means \(94.2\%\) remains and the overall decrease is \(5.8\%\).

sections.title: How do I undo a chain or return to a former amount?
sections.label: Divide by the complete multiplier
sections.intro: When only the final amount is supplied, recover the original by undoing every stage. When restoring one quantity, the current amount is the denominator of the required percentage increase.

blocks.html: If the stage factors are \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), divide the supplied final amount by \(m_1m_2\). Equivalently, undo the last stage first and then the earlier one.

blocks.title: Find the increase that restores the original
blocks.prompt: A vessel's capacity fell from \(3766\) litres to \(2800\) litres. By what percentage must the reduced capacity increase to reach the former capacity? Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.hint: The increase starts at the smaller value. Divide the required gain by that value.
blocks.solution:
The amount to restore is \(3766-2800=966\) litres.

The requested increase is relative to the reduced capacity; \(2800\) goes in the denominator.

\(\frac{966}{2800} imes100=34.5\). So the required increase is \(34.5\%\).

blocks.html: Dividing by just one factor only goes back one step in the process.

blocks.title: Work backwards through two changes
blocks.prompt: The volume of liquid in a test is increased by \(30\%\), then the updated volume decreases by \(28\%\). The final volume is \(4960.8\) litres. Find the volume in litres before either change.
blocks.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is \(1.3\) and the second is \(0.72\).

The combined multiplier is \(1.3\times0.72=0.936\).

Undo the multiplication: \(\frac{4960.8}{0.936}=5300\) litres.

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

blocks.html: Check your recovered initial value by applying the full chain in the forward direction.

examples.title: Apply an increase followed by a decrease
examples.question: The starting volume in a tank is \(2900\) litres. It is increased by \(8\%\), then the updated volume decreases by \(6\%\). Find the final volume in litres.
solution: The first multiplier is \(1.08\) and the second is \(0.94\).

examples.title: Use two decreases on different bases
examples.question: A batch starts with mass \(5400\) kg. Stage 1 reduces its mass by \(20\%\). Stage 2 reduces the remaining mass by \(16\%\). Find the mass after both drying stages in kilograms.
solution: The first multiplier is \(0.8\) and the second is \(0.84\).

examples.title: Calculate the net change after equal rates
examples.question: The size of an image file first increases by \(5\%\). The resulting size then decreases by \(5\%\). Find the overall percentage decrease from the original size.
solution: The first multiplier is \(1.05\) and the second is \(0.95\).
The final value is \(99.75\%\) of the original, so the overall decrease is \(0.25\%\).

examples.title: Interpret the product of two reductions
examples.question: A supplier reduces a packaging fee by \(11.25\%\). The reduced fee is then cut by a further \(28\%\). Find the overall percentage decrease.
solution: The first multiplier is \(0.8875\) and the second is \(0.72\).
The final value is \(63.9\%\) of the original, so the overall decrease is \(36.1\%\).

examples.title: Find the increase that restores the original
examples.question: A vessel's capacity fell from \(5750.5\) litres to \(5300\) litres. By what percentage must the reduced capacity increase to reach the former capacity?
solution: The requested increase is relative to the reduced capacity; \(5300\) goes in the denominator.
\(\frac{450.5}{5300} imes100=8.5\). So the required increase is \(8.5\%\).

examples.question: The volume of liquid in a test is increased by \(28\%\), then the updated volume decreases by \(26\%\). The final volume is \(7388.16\) litres. Find the volume in litres before either change.
solution: The first multiplier is \(1.28\) and the second is \(0.74\).

extraPractice.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.

The first multiplier is \(0.75\) and the second is \(0.77\).

The combined multiplier is \(0.75\times0.77=0.5775\).

\(400\times0.5775=231\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

extraPractice.title: Calculate the net change after equal rates
extraPractice.prompt: The size of an image file first increases by \(7\%\). The resulting size then decreases by \(7\%\). Find the overall percentage decrease from the original size. Enter the number before the percent sign.
extraPractice.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
extraPractice.solution:
The first multiplier is \(1.07\) and the second is \(0.93\).

The combined multiplier is \(1.07\times0.93=0.9951\).

The final value is \(99.51\%\) of the original, so the overall decrease is \(0.49\%\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

extraPractice.title: Interpret the product of two reductions
extraPractice.prompt: A supplier reduces a packaging fee by \(15.25\%\). The reduced fee is then cut by a further \(4\%\). Find the overall percentage decrease. Enter the number before the percent sign.
extraPractice.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
extraPractice.solution:
The first multiplier is \(0.8475\) and the second is \(0.96\).

The combined multiplier is \(0.8475\times0.96=0.8136\).

The final value is \(81.36\%\) of the original, so the overall decrease is \(18.64\%\).

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

extraPractice.title: Find the increase that restores the original
extraPractice.prompt: A vessel's capacity fell from \(381\) litres to \(300\) litres. By what percentage must the reduced capacity increase to reach the former capacity? Enter the number before the percent sign.
extraPractice.hint: The increase starts at the smaller value. Divide the required gain by that value.
extraPractice.solution:
The amount to restore is \(381-300=81\) litres.

The requested increase is relative to the reduced capacity; \(300\) goes in the denominator.

\(\frac{81}{300} imes100=27\). So the required increase is \(27\%\).

extraPractice.title: Work backwards through two changes
extraPractice.prompt: The volume of liquid in a test is increased by \(32\%\), then the updated volume decreases by \(30\%\). The final volume is \(2587.2\) litres. Find the volume in litres before either change.
extraPractice.hint: Every percentage applies to the value at the start of its own stage.
extraPractice.solution:
The first multiplier is \(1.32\) and the second is \(0.7\).

The combined multiplier is \(1.32\times0.7=0.924\).

Undo the multiplication: \(\frac{2587.2}{0.924}=2800\) litres.

retry.feedback: Percentages apply to changing bases. Use both stage multipliers together.

glossary.definition: The percentage difference between the final and starting amounts, based on the start.

revision.body:
Methods

MethodWhat to do
Change the base at each stageMultiply by the first factor, then the second. The single equivalent multiplier is their product.
Compare the product with 1Above 1 means a net increase, and below 1 means a net decrease. Subtract the smaller of the product and 1 from the larger and multiply by 100 for the size of the change.
Divide by the complete multiplierIf the stage factors are \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), divide the supplied final amount by \(m_1m_2\). Equivalently, undo the last stage first and then the earlier one.

Worked line

\(1.16\times0.85=0.986\)

Check yourself

An amount decreases by \(12\%\) and then by \(8\%\). Find the overall decrease.

Answer \(19.04\%\)
revision.checks:
• Adding the rates treats both changes as amounts taken on the same original base. Successive changes normally use different bases.
  • An increase and a decrease at the same rate do not return you to the start. The decrease uses the increased base.
  • Dividing by just one factor only goes back one step in the process.
revision.examTip: Use a product, then say how the final amount compares with the original.
